sections.h2: How Washington property tax is set
sections.html:
The county assessor values every parcel each year, and the county treasurer sends and collects the bill. RCW 84.40.020 has real property listed and assessed every year by its value on January 1.

The standard, from RCW 84.40.030, is 100 percent of true and fair value in money. For a house, the assessor looks first at sales of the property or similar properties within the past five years and must respect existing zoning, so a value cannot rest on a use the land is not allowed to have. Land and structures are valued separately, and together they cannot exceed what the property is worth as it stands.

When your value changes, a notice goes out no later than thirty days after the appraisal (RCW 84.40.045). It shows the old and new value with land and improvements split out, and a short description of how to appeal. No such notice may be mailed between January 15 and February 15.

Taxes are payable in two halves: the first on or before April 30 and the second on or before October 31. RCW 84.56.020 sets the calendar, and splitting the bill applies when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more.

Payment or penaltyDate or rate
First halfDue on or before April 30
Second halfDue on or before October 31
Tax statementsSent by March 15 when budgets, levies and the tax roll arrive on schedule
Interest on a residential parcel with four or fewer units9 percent per year, computed monthly from delinquency, with no penalty
Interest on other property12 percent per year
Penalties on nonresidential, larger multifamily and personal property3 percent on tax delinquent June 1, plus 8 percent more on December 1

A payment mailed without a readable postmark, or made through an automated check service, counts as on time if it arrives within three business days of the due date. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements and take partial payments, applied to the oldest delinquent year first unless you ask otherwise. Call your county treasurer to learn which options are available.

File a petition with your county board of equalization on the state form. RCW 84.40.038 gives you whichever of these dates is latest:

  • July 1 of the year of the assessment.
  • Thirty days after the assessment or value change notice was mailed.
  • Thirty days after the assessor sent it electronically or told you it was available online.
  • A county-adopted window of up to sixty days.

A petition that is not on the prescribed form or is incomplete may be refused, so read the form before you send it. A late filing can be excused if you file within a reasonable time and show good cause. Examples in the statute include a death or serious illness in the family, being away from your mailing address for more than fifteen of the allowed days when the deadline falls after July 1, wrong written advice from county staff, a flood or earthquake, or a documented postal delay. The board must waive the deadline if no revaluation notice was ever sent to you although your area was revalued and your value did not change.

You and the assessor can ask for a direct appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals if the assessor, you and a majority of the county board all agree. The state board may decline, and the county board then hears the case. The Board of Tax Appeals publishes appeal forms and a checklist for residential owners who go beyond the county board.

If a bill comes due while your appeal is still open, ask the county treasurer how to handle the payment.

Three programs stand out: an exemption, a deferral, and a grant for the surviving spouse of a veteran. The Department of Revenue describes each on its exemptions and deferrals page, and your county assessor takes the applications.

  • Senior, disability and veteran exemption. You must own and occupy your primary residence in Washington with income at or below your county's threshold. You must also be at least 61 by December 31 of the assessment year, unable to work because of a disability, or a veteran with a qualifying VA rating. The reduction depends on income, home value and local levy rates, and the assessor decides how often you renew, at least once every six years.
  • Senior and disability deferral. Open to owner-occupants who are 60 or older, or retired because of disability, with enough equity to secure the state's interest. Deferred tax accrues 5 percent simple interest and is repaid when the home is sold, the owner dies, or the home stops being the primary residence.
  • Widow or widower of a veteran. A grant that need not be repaid if the recipient lives in the home until at least December 15 of the year it is received.

Two protections sit in the collection statutes. A treasurer may not sell a property that is eligible for deferral and must instead require the owner to file a declaration to defer (RCW 84.64.050(6)). And under RCW 84.56.020(19), an income-qualified owner living in a home already facing tax foreclosure can have outstanding interest and penalties waived once, starting about 60 days before the three-year mark.

Income limits differ by county, so ask the county assessor for your county's current threshold before deciding whether to apply.

Interest runs from the date of delinquency, and after three years the county moves toward foreclosure. RCW 84.64.050 directs the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency once three years have run from the date of delinquency, then foreclose the tax liens in the county's name. The owner and anyone with a recorded interest receive notice and have thirty days after service to appear and defend or pay what is due.

Before any sale, the treasurer runs a title search to confirm the legal description and the record titleholder, who is treated as the owner for notice purposes. A certificate of delinquency is barred when the total delinquency is $100 or less, not counting interest and penalties, except on parcels a local government has declared a nuisance.

Treasurers must also tell delinquent owners where to get help, including the statewide foreclosure hotline recommended by the Washington State Housing Finance Commission. Roughly two years into a delinquency, the treasurer passes the owner's name and address to a homeownership resource center or other designated entity.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed, and excise tax at closing
sections.html:
The tax lien runs from January 1, so the year's bill follows the property until paid. RCW 84.60.020 makes the seller liable, when the sale agreement is silent, for the share of that year's tax matching the part of the calendar year before the day of sale, with the buyer taking the rest. Most contracts set their own split, and escrow normally settles it at closing. If you owe back taxes, ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure that includes interest through the closing date.

A sale also triggers the real estate excise tax. The REET page of the Department of Revenue explains that the seller usually pays, the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and an unpaid balance can become a lien on the property. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state portion is 1.1 percent of the price up to $551,000, 1.28 percent from there to $1,551,000, 2.75 percent to $3,051,000, and 3 percent above that. Local excise tax is added, and interest runs on unpaid tax after one month. The settlement statement will show the exact figure.

If you need to move fast with taxes owed, repairs pending or a tenant in place, a cash buyer can price those items into an as-is offer. The tax payoff appears as a line item, so you see exactly what comes out of your proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal my Washington property value?
faqs.a: It is the latest of July 1, thirty days after the notice was mailed or sent electronically, or a county-adopted window of up to sixty days. The county board of equalization can excuse a late filing for good cause, such as serious illness, a flood or a documented postal delay.

faqs.q: Can I pay Washington property tax in two payments?
faqs.a: Yes, when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more. Half is due by April 30 and the rest by October 31. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements or partial payments, so ask yours what is available.

faqs.q: How much interest do late Washington property taxes carry?
faqs.a: A residential parcel with four or fewer units pays 9 percent a year, computed monthly, with no penalty. Other property pays 12 percent, and nonresidential property, larger multifamily buildings and personal property also face a 3 percent penalty on June 1 and 8 percent more on December 1.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay property tax if I qualify for a senior exemption or deferral?
faqs.a: An exemption lowers what you owe, based on income, home value and levy rates. A deferral postpones payment at 5 percent simple interest, due when the home is sold, the owner dies, or it stops being the primary residence. Your county assessor handles both applications.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax at closing when I sell my house in Washington?
faqs.a: The sale agreement decides. If it is silent, the seller owes the share of the year's tax matching the days before the sale and the buyer owes the rest. Escrow usually works this out on the settlement statement, alongside the seller's real estate excise tax.
